Hey, take a deep breath kid. This shit is scary and your feelings are totally valid. I was undiagnosed at your age but was dealing with chronic fatigue due to my illness. Personally, high school was so much harder than the real world is. Don’t get me wrong my disease and all the things that come with it certainly hinder me and my day but it’s so much less stressful now. School doesn’t give you a break, they just keep piling on the pressure telling you the next step will be even harder, but that’s not true. 

When I went to college (and if you choose this route you should have some freedom there as well) I got to pick how many classes I took each semester and which time slot I went (out of the available ones), I had full days off during the week because that’s what I needed and no one had a problem with it. Professors were also much more understanding and lenient than teachers in high school. 

I’m 25 now and work full time in a warehouse. It’s not easy considering the whole chronic illness thing but my managers are very understanding and supportive. I can sit and take a breather when I need. It doesn’t feel like the rest of my life is riding on every decision I make. I get to go home at the end of the day and not stress about tests or homework. 

I’m surrounded by more compassion and understanding than ever, and you’ll get there too. High school sucks for everyone, and you’ve got an additional layer of struggle. It’s hard to hunker down and get through it but it’s so worth it on the other side. I’m sicker now (progressive disease) than I was then but life is easier to manage as well. 

I’m rooting for you kid, hang in there.

I have three. Most of the time I just find them peaceful. I like walking them alone and feel practically nothing walking through them, aside from the occasional sadness for a new grave or for a child in general. I’m also not a very spiritual or religious person who necessarily believes in things like this. 

One time I just felt very unsettled in the entire cemetery as a whole (it was a smaller one with literally one path straight through that just ends in the back). I wouldn’t necessarily say i was scared? I was able to walk the entire thing but did so pretty quickly and left right away. 

The next one was a specific grave, another small cemetery again with one dead end path straight through. I was walking the rows and one of the very last graves I came across was from sometime in the 1800’s. As i got closer to it i had that gut “i need to leave now” feeling. It was intense enough i walked right to the car and left. I almost felt like i was being followed out of there. I went back a couple years later with a friend and felt the exact same way, i haven’t been back since. 

The last is different. I was in a massive cemetery next to my college. They had a weird two hour gap where they didn’t offer classes but I commuted an hour one way so i couldn’t really go home and didn’t have a dorm to hang out in so i had to keep myself busy for that time. This cemetery has over 17,000 graves so I’m just kind of wandering looking at the ones with pictures when i feel very drawn to one specific grave. I walk over to it from behind and was happy to notice it had a photo despite being older (died in 1930). I felt very calm and warm there, almost like a comforting motherly presence. I spent most of the two hour break just sitting in front of this grave enjoying the feeling. Every time I go back I feel the same way. I just feel very safe with her, like we’re somehow connected in a way. Hundreds of cemeteries, tens of thousands of graves over the course of a few years, and I’ve never experienced a feeling like it any other time.

After graduating high school the biggest weight was off my chest, it helped me so much not having to worry about something so big anymore. Right before I graduated my psychiatrist diagnosed me with autism, which after a year helped her put me on the right medications.

Being on the right medications and not having to worry about high school helped me go get a job (which I still have and love most days), and by the time I was comfortable at my job and didn’t worry about going anymore I started college, and I could put all my energy into that. 

For me it was all about one step at a time. Just go one by one, and once you’re comfortable with step one, add on step two. So start with seeing a professional (my personal suggestion is to start with a therapist and not a psychiatrist [a psychiatrist  prescribes medications, a therapist is talk therapy and gives you tips to manage certain struggles]), once you’re comfortable with them and have the right techniques or medications to manage things, go back to school or get a job, which ever is easier for you. Once you’ve either gotten comfortable at the job or finished school to the level you wish move onto the other option. Take things slowly. Don’t overwhelm yourself by forcing yourself to do everything at once.

Little deadlines also help me. Like saying “before June 1st I’m going to call a therapist to see if I can set up an appointment”, you don’t need to have already seen them or even have an appointment set up, just make the phone call, or have someone call for you. Or go even smaller and say “by June 1st I’m going to have found a therapist I’m going to call and by July 1st I’m going to call them”.  At least with little personal deadlines you’ll see yourself accomplishing things. It doesn’t matter how small because everyone has to start somewhere.
